transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-11-30 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (CTO, Nightingale), Tom Ortiz (ML Engineer), Leah Brooks (Product)

Auto-generated sections (may be rough):
Topics: per-token pricing, batching, dedicated vs hosted, private deploys, benchmarking
Action Items (summary): Alex to send pricing spreadsheet; Daniel to propose bench plan; Maya to share traffic profile

Transcript:
00:00 Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account. Quick sound check?
00:05 Maya Singh: Hi Alex, yeah loud and clear. Maya here.
00:06 Tom Ortiz: Tom — all good.
00:08 Daniel Park: Daniel from Redwood SE, good afternoon.
00:10 Leah Brooks: Leah, thanks for scheduling.
00:12 Alex Chen: Cool. Today the goal is to understand your cost constraints and how you'd prefer to run inference — hosted API to start, or a longer-term dedicated or private setup — and what success looks like for a pilot. We can go deep on unit economics.
00:24 Maya Singh: Great. To frame it — we have a patient-summarization product in beta, expecting 10k monthly active clinicians initially, average of, say, 20 prompts per user per month, with variable prompt lengths. We're concerned about runaway costs if we just do pay-as-you-go. The security/compliance side will need SOC 2 and KMS. Also low p95 latency for interactive use.
00:45 Alex Chen: Perfect. Can you confirm average tokens per prompt and completion, or is that what you're not sure about?
00:50 Tom Ortiz: We're still instrumenting but rough numbers — ~120 tokens input, ~220 tokens output per call on average. Some long summaries hit 800-1k tokens for a minority.
01:02 Daniel Park: That's helpful. Okay so baseline traffic math: 10k MAU * 20 prompts = 200k calls/month, at ~340 tokens total per call -> about 68M tokens/month. If we used hosted per-token pricing, we can ballpark cost, but reserved/dedicated will probably move the needle if you want predictability.
01:20 Leah Brooks: How big a delta are we talking between hosted per-token and reserved? Our CFO wants monthly spend not spiky bills.
01:26 Alex Chen: Short answer: it's workload dependent. Hosted per-token gives zero ops but higher unit cost; Dedicated (reserved capacity) has a fixed monthly commitment that amortizes GPU costs and can be materially cheaper per token at scale — sometimes 30-60% depending on model size, batching utilization, and KV caching hit rate.
01:42 Maya Singh: KV caching hit rate? 
01:44 Daniel Park: Yeah — prefix caching / KV cache. For your use case if clinicians query similar patient metadata and you can cache responses or prefixes, you get large effective savings — fewer tokens emitted and better throughput with batching. We also do automatic continuous batching; the more parallel requests we can pack into a GPU batch, the lower latency per token and lower cost. But batching also trades off with tail latency.
02:05 Tom Ortiz: So if we have tight p95 latency constraints for interactive use, does batching hurt us?
02:10 Daniel Park: It depends on your latency SLO. We tune batching windows (ms) per route. For sub-200ms p95 you often accept smaller batches and higher unit cost. For background jobs or async summarization you can push bigger windows. We can show sample configs.
02:25 Maya Singh: For CFO speak — give me an example: 68M tokens/month — what's ballpark dollars on hosted vs dedicated?
02:32 Alex Chen: I can do a quick back-of-envelope. Hosted per-token at list (example) $0.0003 per token (note: we will send a tailored sheet) -> 68M * 0.0003 = $20.4k/month. But that list per-token is for a mid-sized open model; higher-capacity models can be more. Dedicated reserved can drop effective per-token to say $0.00012-$0.00018 depending on commit and model. So maybe $8k-$12k/month at same quality, but you have to commit to a monthly capacity and there's onboarding.
03:05 Leah Brooks: That seems promising. What's the commit level we need to get that discount?
03:09 Alex Chen: Typically you sign for a dedicated GPU pool — e.g., a 2x A100 equivalent reserved for you. The exact commit is negotiable but historically customers with 50-200M tokens/month see strong wins. We'll propose tiers in the spreadsheet.
03:22 Tom Ortiz: What about private deployment — we have data residency requirements for some clients — is pricing similar?
03:28 Daniel Park: Private (VPC/on-prem) is usually licensed — platform fee plus support, and you'd cover infra costs. Unit economics are then determined by your infra efficiency and our runtime optimizations. For some customers that's cheaper long-term if you already have GPU capacity and ops team. There's also the security upside: private control plane, KMS/HSM integration.
03:45 Maya Singh: Okay. Another question — we are also considering quantized models to cut cost further. How much does quantization impact quality for summarization?
03:52 Daniel Park: 8-bit or 4-bit quantization often preserves quality for many LMs especially when combined with post-training calibration and evals. We'll propose a small eval sweep in the bench. Quantization reduces memory and allows denser packing, which can lower per-token cost on dedicated infra. But you need to validate on your prompts.
04:12 Alex Chen: Worth noting for finances — caching and prefixing can be the single biggest lever if you can share context across requests. Even a 20% effective token reduction is a 20% cost cut.
04:22 Leah Brooks: If we do a pilot, what does the pilot look like operationally?
04:26 Alex Chen: Pilot options: 1) Hosted pilot — quick sign-up, scoped traffic capped to X rps, Redwood provides logs and cost breakdowns. 2) Reserved short-term pilot — reserved capacity for 30-60 days, we run benchmarks and assess utilization. 3) Private trial — more involved, we do a light private deploy in your VPC for an eval. For discovery, we usually recommend hosted pilot to get prompt-level regressions and cost visibility, then move to reserved/dedicated once you have throughput.
04:52 Maya Singh: We prefer predictable spend so maybe a short reserved pilot is interesting. What about autoscaling and burst capacity? We have weekly peaks at end of day.
04:59 Daniel Park: On Dedicated we offer configurable autoscale policies with burst buckets. You can set soft limits, guaranteed throughput, and overflow to hosted tiers if desired. That way spikes don't fail, but cost and SLAs vary with policy.
05:15 Tom Ortiz: Any gotchas on measuring unit-econ? Like tokenization differences between SDKs?
05:19 Daniel Park: Good callout — tokenization differences, system prompts, and response trimming matter. We instrument token counts at the route level and will give you token-level breakdowns including prompt vs completion. Also include per-token compute (GPU seconds) in the dashboard so you can map tokens to cost.
05:36 Leah Brooks: Security — SOC2, SAML, audit logs. How mature is Redwood there?
05:41 Alex Chen: We are SOC 2 compliant — we'll send the security pack. SAML/SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integrations are all supported. For private/on-prem we do HSM support via customer KMS.
05:55 Maya Singh: That helps. On billing — do we get daily burn reports?
05:58 Alex Chen: Yes, the Console exposes token-level cost, per-route breakdowns, and near-real-time usage analytics. We'll include sample screenshots in the follow-up.
06:08 Tom Ortiz: Benchmarking — how long and what do you need from us?
06:11 Daniel Park: For a representative bench we need a sample prompt set (real or anonymized), expected concurrency profile (p50/p95 latency targets), and any QoS constraints. We'll run multiple model variants, batching configs, and quantization options. We'll provide p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec throughput, and cost per 1M tokens for each config.
06:33 Maya Singh: Timeframe?
06:34 Alex Chen: If you share prompts and traffic by Thursday, Daniel's team can run a bench early next week and present results mid-next week.
06:42 Leah Brooks: Pricing model question — can we have a blended approach? Some high-sensitivity routes run on Private and the rest on Hosted?
06:48 Daniel Park: Absolutely. Smart routing policies let you route by route or by policy — region, tier, sensitivity. You can also do automatic fallback to smaller/cheaper model variants on congestion.
06:58 Maya Singh: Any references of customers who did a hybrid approach?
06:59 Alex Chen: Yes — a healthcare customer did private for PHI processing and hosted for general summarization; they used caching and prefixing to keep hosted costs down. We can share an anonymized case study.
07:10 Tom Ortiz: About latency during heavy batching — will p95 blow up?
07:12 Daniel Park: Not if you set a max latency window and allow smaller batches for low-latency routes. We tune continuous batching and have kernel selection that helps for variable sequence lengths. But yeah, naive large batches can increase p95.
07:26 Leah Brooks: For our pilot runway: do we need any legal/PO before starting a hosted pilot?
07:30 Alex Chen: Hosted pilot can start with a standard SaaS agreement; for enterprise-level reserved/dedicated or private we'll need an MSA and SOW. Procurement usually asks for security docs — we'll send them.
07:40 Maya Singh: Cool. Let's do the steps you proposed.
07:42 Alex Chen: Recap then: Alex will send a tailored pricing spreadsheet with hosted per-token numbers and reserved tiers, Daniel will produce a bench plan with suggested batching and quantization configs, and Nightingale will share the prompt set and traffic profile. We schedule a 2-hr bench kickoff next week. Any other asks?
07:58 Maya Singh: Please include assumptions for cache hit rates and batching efficiency in the pricing model — those are the biggest uncertainty.
08:06 Daniel Park: Will do. We'll include conservative, expected, and aggressive scenarios (e.g., 10/30/50% caching hit).
08:12 Tom Ortiz: Also include model variant comparisons — smaller model that meets quality bar vs larger which is higher cost.
08:17 Alex Chen: Noted.
08:19 Leah Brooks: Ok thanks all. That was helpful.
08:22 Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with docs and proposed slots for the bench.
08:25 Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional overlap and noise; some product names may be mis-transcribed.
